workload.description: 50k ID/s; Snowflake-style in-process generation - no database anywhere on the request path

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: c7g.large — AWS EC2 us-east-1 / On-Demand / Linux / shared tenancy / 730 h per month; instance-hour only (excludes EBS, data transfer); arm64 (Graviton3). Band: zero-width: within the pinned scope the hourly list rate is a single exact published number with no variance. Month length (672-744 h), burstable credit surcharges, Savings Plans and Spot are OUT-OF-BAND modifiers, named per row, not band edges.

citations.note: $0.0725/h x 730 = 5293c/month. Cross-checked to the cent against the AWS Price List Bulk API (version 20260904231117).

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: cache.t4g.medium — AWS ElastiCache us-east-1 / On-Demand / Redis engine / standard support / 730 h per month; node-hour only. Band: zero-width at the Redis/Memcached standard-support rate. The Valkey engine is CHEAPER and Extended Support is DEARER; both are different products/support states, not a price range for this row, so they are named here rather than used as band edges.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 50,000 IDs/s peak. Snowflake generation is a single server-side operation, so the call mix is deliberately almost flat: 99.8% generate_id, 0.2% worker introspection. The introspection flow is not invented - the archived 2010 Twitter Snowflake API exposed get_worker_id, get_timestamp and get_datacenter_id alongside get_id, and operators and bootstrapping clients call them. The previous version of this file used a 97/2/1 split whose 2% 'reserve_block' flow belonged to a DIFFERENT algorithm (see the `algorithm` assumption) and has been removed rather than re-weighted. The 0.2% introspection share is a modelling estimate: no public Snowflake call-mix breakdown exists, so nothing here should be read as a measured ratio.

assumptions.subject: algorithm
assumptions.statement: This file commits to ONE algorithm: Twitter Snowflake (64-bit time|datacenter|worker|sequence), minted in process with no coordination per ID. The archived 2010 README specifies 'sequence number - 12 bits - rolls over every 4096 per machine', so a worker mints IDs locally and never fetches a range from anywhere. The previous version also modelled a Postgres 'segment allocator' handing out 1,000-ID blocks on the generate path; block allocation is the OTHER family - Flickr's 2010 ticket servers (REPLACE INTO plus LAST_INSERT_ID() across two MySQL boxes split odd/even by auto-increment-offset) and Meituan Leaf's segment mode, whose README makes leaf.segment.enable (a MySQL leaf_alloc table) and leaf.snowflake.enable (ZooKeeper for workId, no database at all) independently switchable ALTERNATIVES. Welding the two together put a database on a hot path that in this design has none, and it is why the old file pointed at the wrong component. The sql_db segment allocator and its read replica have therefore been deleted, not re-weighted. If you want the segment/ticket-server design instead, it has a different shape and a different binding constraint, and this blueprint will not tell you where that constraint is.

assumptions.subject: app
assumptions.statement: Re-rated from 6,000 to 25,000 rps per node on a 2-vCPU c7g.large. ID generation is pure in-process arithmetic with no network hop on the hot path, so a node is bound by request handling, not by the ID math. Meituan Leaf's README publishes 'On the basis of 4C8G VM, through the company RPC method, QPS pressure test results are nearly 5w/s, TP999 1ms' - 50,000 QPS on 4 cores is 12,500 per core, so 2 vCPU scales to roughly 25,000. Twitter's own 2010 README set a floor of 'minimum 10k ids per second per process'. The old 6,000 figure was 3,000 per core, below BOTH published numbers, and that single wrong number is what made this file name the wrong bottleneck. base_latency_ms is left at 0.8 ms, consistent with Leaf's published TP999 of 1 ms. This is a figure scaled from someone else's benchmark on different hardware and a different RPC stack, not a measurement of this design, so the component stays ASSUMPTION and is not promoted to GROUNDED.

assumptions.subject: lb
assumptions.statement: The L4 load-balancer tier is a 2-unit N+1 pair, each rated to absorb the full 50,000 rps alone so either unit can carry the design load if its peer fails. That deliberate redundancy, not a capacity shortfall, is why this tier runs where it does relative to the others - and it is the honest headline of the whole design: at 50k IDs/s a standalone ID service is network-bound, not CPU-bound. The work is moving 50,000 request/response pairs per second, not computing 50,000 shifts and masks. The 50,000 rps per-unit rating is an ASSUMPTION: no vendor-published per-unit L4 throughput figure is cited here, and none was found.

assumptions.subject: app_fleet
assumptions.statement: 12 nodes are kept even though the fleet now sits far below its capacity ceiling at this load. The node count is set by availability and worker-id spread - zone spread, rolling restarts, and one distinct worker id per process - not by throughput: a Snowflake fleet is sized so that losing a zone does not lose the ID service. The engine computes both the resulting utilisation and the resulting monthly bill; read both, because this over-provision is a real cost and a smaller fleet would still carry the stated load.

assumptions.subject: coord
assumptions.statement: Worker-ID lease is checked at startup and heartbeated, not per request; modelled as a 5% visit on the generate path. etcd is modelled with the `cache` kind - Keystone v1 has no dedicated coordination-store kind, and a KV store is the closest honest shape. With the segment-allocator database removed, this registry is the design's only remote dependency, which matches Leaf's snowflake mode: it uses ZooKeeper for workId and touches no database. The 5% remains a modelling stand-in for a startup/heartbeat concern, so the arrival rate the engine computes for this component is not a measurement of anything real.

assumptions.subject: algorithmic_ceiling
assumptions.statement: The bit layout is itself a capacity ceiling, and it is the only capacity number in this file with a hard published source. Twitter Snowflake's 12-bit sequence 'rolls over every 4096 per machine' per millisecond, which is 4,096,000 IDs/s per worker. Sony's Sonyflake trades rate for lifetime with a 39/8/16 layout and states the consequence outright: '2^8 IDs per 10 msec at most in a single instance', which is 25,600/s per machine. On Sonyflake's layout the algorithmic ceiling and the per-node request-handling rate assumed above are essentially the same number, so the layout you choose can become the binding constraint before your CPUs do. This blueprint models Snowflake's layout, where the algorithmic ceiling sits far above the modelled load - and the engine does not model bit layouts at all, so it will never surface this as a bottleneck. You have to check it yourself.

assumptions.subject: shape
assumptions.statement: The load-balancer-plus-service-nodes shape modelled here is the 2010 Twitter shape, and it is no longer how most teams solve this. The twitter-archive/snowflake repository is archived (2021-09-18) with the note 'We have retired the initial release of Snowflake'. Instagram skipped the service entirely and put generation inside the database - 'We've delegated ID creation to each table inside each shard, by using PL/PGSQL' - explicitly because 'the additional complexity required to run an ID service was a point against it'. Modern practice is an embedded library in the calling process, which deletes the load balancer, the app tier, and therefore this blueprint's entire bottleneck. Use this file to learn where a standalone ID SERVICE binds; do not read it as a recommendation to build one.

assumptions.subject: clock
assumptions.statement: Snowflake correctness depends on monotonic wall-clock time. Clock skew / leap-second stalls are a CORRECTNESS failure mode, not a capacity one, and the v1 analytical engine cannot model them - it computes throughput and latency only. Treat NTP discipline and the reject-on-backwards-clock guard as an unmodelled requirement.

assumptions.subject: lb
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED: the engine reasons in requests per second. An L4 load balancer's real limits are new connections per second, packets per second and bandwidth, none of which this model represents. Its utilisation here is a proxy - useful for deciding WHICH tier binds first, not a number to size network hardware from.

assumptions.subject: decode
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED: decoding a Snowflake ID back into its timestamp, datacenter and worker fields is a shift and a mask performed by the CLIENT, so it generates no server traffic and no longer appears as a flow. The previous version routed a 'decode_id' flow through a read replica, which billed a second database for arithmetic that never leaves the caller's process; that replica has been deleted. If your product genuinely looks up metadata BY id, that is a separate service with its own datastore, and it is not modelled here - add it before trusting this bottleneck or this cost.

assumptions.subject: coord
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED: worker-id uniqueness. Two processes holding or configured with the same worker id will mint duplicate IDs at full rate, and no utilisation, latency or cost figure in this report changes when that happens. The coordination store exists for correctness, not throughput - sizing it from the arrival rate the engine computes for it would be reading the wrong signal entirely. Lease expiry, split-brain on the registry, and the blast radius of a duplicate id are all outside the engine.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED: burst shape below the second. Peak is entered as a flat 50,000 rps, but a Snowflake worker's sequence saturates at MILLISECOND granularity - exhausting the 4,096 sequence slots inside a single millisecond makes the worker spin-wait for the next tick, adding latency that a per-second average cannot show. Any sub-second spike behaviour is invisible in these figures.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED: the load-balancer tier carries a per-instance cost of zero because Keystone has no grounded per-instance price for that kind, and inventing one would be worse than declaring the gap. A real L4 load balancer at this rate is billed on hours plus processed bytes/connections, so the monthly total below is a FLOOR for the network tier, not a full bill.

_library.summary: Snowflake-style service that hands out globally unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs at high rate, with no database on the request path.
